chunks: Controlling BLDC motors. The question: How do you control BLDC motors?
Controlling a BLDC motor has three layers. First, work out which coils to power, based on where the rotor (the spinning magnet) is.
Second, use PWM to set how much voltage the coils get. Third, run control loops on speed and current.
Six-step is the simple method; field-oriented control is the smooth, efficient one.
Think of pushing a child on a swing. You need to push at the right moment in the swing, which means watching where the swing is. That is commutation, with a sensor as your eyes.
How hard you push sets how high the swing goes. That is the voltage or current.
The analogy has one gap: a motor needs a push in a new direction six times per electrical turn, not just once per swing.
Everything in BLDC control fits this loop. Position feedback feeds both commutation (fast) and the speed loop (slow).
Current feedback closes the inner loop and doubles as the overcurrent protection.
Commutation: choosing which of the three coil groups (phases) to power as the rotor turns. PWM: switching the supply on and off very fast.
The fraction of time it is on, the duty, sets the average voltage. Hall sensor: a position sensor, so the controller knows the rotor's sector.
Six-step control: a simple method that powers two phases at a time from a lookup table. Field-oriented control (FOC): a smoother method that controls the current's angle and size.
Say a motor runs from a 24 volts supply. Three Hall sensors each report on or off, and together they tell the controller which of six sectors the rotor is in.
A lookup table then says which two phases to power. If the PWM duty is 50%, the coils see an average of 12 volts, so the motor runs at about half speed.
A control loop measures the speed and nudges that duty up or down to hold the speed you asked for.
That is the whole idea: read the position, switch the phases, and PWM the voltage.
"I think in three layers. Commutation chooses the active phases from rotor position, using Hall sensors, back-EMF zero-crossings or an encoder.
Modulation uses PWM on a three-phase bridge to set the voltage. On top are a current loop and a speed loop.

The simple version is six-step with Hall sensors, which is cheap but has torque ripple; the high-performance version is field-oriented control, which regulates the d and q currents for smooth, efficient torque."
